shower.thought: We spend our whole lives learning how to be ourselves, but we're never sure if we actually succeeded.
Time moves slower when you're waiting for something because your brain is checking more often—you're literally experiencing more moments.
You can't remember most of your life, but it still shaped who you are, like a sculpture carved by invisible hands.
The scariest part about getting older isn't death—it's realizing how little you understand about being alive.
Every conversation you have is half you trying to explain yourself and half you imagining how they're interpreting you.
You've probably forgotten the single most important advice someone ever gave you.
Nostalgia is just your brain editing the past to match your mood better than it actually was.
If you had to teach someone how to be human, you'd realize you don't actually know.
The people you miss the most are often the ones you didn't appreciate while they were here.
You've never seen your own face—not really. You've only ever seen its reflection or a flattened image.
Comfort is the enemy of growth, which is why happiness and progress are almost never the same thing.
Your childhood best friend became a stranger slowly enough that you didn't notice the exact moment it happened.
We say "I have no idea" when we mean we have no answer, but we're usually full of ideas—just not the right ones.
The saddest part about getting what you want is realizing you wanted the wrong thing all along.
You're more similar to a stranger than you are different, yet that small difference is all you can see.
Overthinking isn't your brain trying to solve the problem—it's your brain afraid of being quiet.
Most of what you believe about yourself isn't based on evidence; it's based on a handful of moments you misinterpreted.
The fact that you're aware you're going to die might actually be your greatest advantage, not your biggest burden.
You keep trying to be someone, when what the world actually needs is for you to stop trying.
Regret is just your brain running a simulation of alternate lives and choosing to be sad about the one you're actually living.

darkjoke.thought:
I told my wife she was drawing her eyebrows too high.
She looked surprised.

My grandfather said, "Your generation is too reliant on technology."
I unplugged his life support to prove him wrong.

I'm reading a book on the history of glue.
I can't put it down.

My friend said he was going to commit suicide.
I said, "You'll have to get in line."
I used to be addicted to soap, but I'm clean now.

My therapist asked how I felt about my childhood.
I said, "I'm not paying you to make me sad about things I've already forgotten."

I told my friend he was drawing his life conclusions too early.
Turns out he was just hanging around.

Dating a vegan is great.
More meat for me.

My dad jokes that he's invisible.
No one's ever heard of him.
I have a stepladder because my real ladder left when I was just a kid.

My wife accused me of being emotionally unavailable.
I didn't respond because I was busy not caring.

I told my boss I needed a mental health day.
He said I needed several.

They say money can't buy happiness.
But it can buy a jet ski. Have you ever seen someone frown on a jet ski?
You probably have—that was me realizing I'd spent my daughter's college fund.

My friend asked if I believed in life after death.
I said, "I don't know, but based on my dating history, I believe in suffering before it."
I'm not saying I'm a terrible parent, but my kid's imaginary friend moved out.

My therapist asked what my biggest fear was.
I said, "Becoming my father."
She said, "You already have."

I told my son he was adopted.
He cried for three hours.
The joke's on him—he's not.

People say I'm too negative.
I disagree. I think they're just too optimistic.

I asked my mom why she never calls.
She said, "I do call. I just hang up when you answer."

My doctor told me I need to watch my drinking.
So now I drink in front of a mirror.
